draft.title: Electron configuration
card: Electrons sit in energy levels (shells) around the nucleus. Each level has subshells called s, p and d. An s subshell holds up to 2 electrons, a p subshell up to 6 and a d subshell up to 10.
Electrons fill the lowest energy subshell first. The order starts 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d. Note that 4s fills before 3d.
A configuration lists the subshells and their electrons. Sodium has 11 electrons, so its configuration is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹.
The electrons in the outermost energy level are the valence electrons. They decide how an element reacts. Atoms with the same number of valence electrons often react in similar ways.
draft.remember: Fill from the lowest energy up. The outer electrons decide how an atom reacts.

a.q: Which is the correct electron configuration of a neutral magnesium atom, which has 12 electrons?
opts: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹ 3p¹
1s² 2s² 2p⁸ 3s¹
1s² 2s² 2p⁴ 3s² 3p²
a.why: The lowest subshells fill first: 1s², 2s², 2p⁶ use 10 electrons, and the last 2 go into 3s. The option with 3s¹ 3p¹ puts an electron in 3p before 3s is full, and a p subshell cannot hold 8 electrons.
a.clue: Fill each subshell to its limit before moving on.

b.q: Sodium has the configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹. Why does it react in a similar way to potassium, which ends in 4s¹?
opts: Both have one electron in their outer energy level
Both have the same number of energy levels
Both have the same total number of electrons
Both have a full outer energy level
b.why: Reactions depend on the outer electrons, and both atoms have one valence electron. They have different numbers of energy levels and total electrons, and neither outer level is full.
b.clue: Look at the last subshell in each configuration.

b.best: Both have one electron in their outer energy level

problems.detail: "Each level has subshells called s, p and d" is false. Level 1 has only an s subshell and level 2 has only s and p; d subshells start at level 3. The card should say which subshells each level has, or say that higher levels add more subshell types.

Why (a) runs two options into one sentence: "The option with 3s¹ 3p¹ ... and a p subshell cannot hold 8 electrons". The 8-electron error belongs to a different option (2p⁸ 3s¹), so students may be confused. The why also never explains what is wrong with the 2p⁴ 3s² 3p² option.

check.summary: The card wrongly says every energy level has s, p and d subshells; level 1 has only s and level 2 has only s and p. Both questions are sound, but why (a) mixes up two wrong options in one sentence.
